items.title: Localized high-Q resonances enable electrically defined beam steering in lithium niobate metasurfaces
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-speed beam steering for LiDAR and optical communication requires independent, reconfigurable control of optical phase. We demonstrate a metasurface combining lithium niobate's Pockels effect with high-Q (Q > 1700) silicon guided-mode resonance nanoantennas whose localized resonances allow individual electro-optic control at a 1 $\mu$m pitch. Identical arrays steer light to 53.5$^\circ$ or 32.4$^\circ$, with the angle set by the bias pattern rather than antenna geometry. We measure 18.0% 0th-order modulation depth, 0.09% of incident power in the steered order, and a 940 MHz detected modulation bandwidth. Mode-overlap analysis shows how inter-element coupling limits usable Q, providing design rules for compact, high-speed beam steering.

items.title: Monte Carlo Framework for Physics-Based Design and Optimization of X-Ray Compressive Ghost Imaging Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: X-ray ghost imaging has emerged as a promising computational imaging modality capable of forming images from spatially integrated measurements. Unlike optical implementations, image formation is governed by multiple energy-dependent photon-matter interactions: photoelectric absorption, Compton scattering, and fluorescence. The relative contributions of these interactions depend on the source spectrum, sample geometry and composition, and detector configuration. We present a FLUKA-based Monte Carlo framework that models photon transport and predicts bucket signals generated by binary illumination patterns. The framework couples a physical scaling analysis, which converts the simulated bucket signals into photon numbers, tube loading and absorbed dose, with a ghost imaging reconstruction analysis of image quality and convergence. Our framework helps assess whether a given configuration is limited by the source output, the mask modulation or the reconstruction before any measurement is made. We evaluate the reconstruction for a centimeter-scale imaging system for an iron crown using one transmission detector and three off-axis scattering detectors over a range of source spectra. The results reveal how source characteristics and detector geometry influence reconstruction quality and radiation dose, providing quantitative guidelines for future X-ray ghost imaging system design. More broadly, this work establishes a predictive design framework for application-specific X-ray ghost imaging systems.

items.title: Machine Learning Surrogate Model for Accelerating InGaAs/GaAs Quantum Well Laser Design
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A machine-learning surrogate model based on a multi-layer perceptron neural network is used to predict six laser performance metrics for an indium gallium arsenide quantum well laser given epitaxial layer parameters as inputs. The surrogate model was trained on simulation data from a set of 4999 designs which were generated by varying epitaxial layer parameters and simulating each design with Harold to extract performance metrics. The model predicts all 6 chosen metrics with a coefficient of determination, $R^2$, greater than 0.91 on a held-out test set and demonstrates a $\sim 10^6 \times$ speed up compared to full device simulations. The model is used to search across 1 million potential epitaxial designs in the parameter space and find designs that minimize threshold current and internal loss. Using the surrogate, rather than full device simulation, reduces computation time for a million designs from 231 days to $\sim$2 minutes on a standard laptop. It is also demonstrated that use of the Swish activation function, rather than ReLU, together with engineered input features - i.e. derived quantities calculated from the base model inputs - raise the mean $R^2$ from 0.88 to 0.94 without additional training data, and reduce the mean absolute percentage error from $1.78 \pm 0.08 \%$ to $1.17 \pm 0.09 \%$.

items.title: Ablation-Driven Selective Laser Direct Mass Transfer for Micro-LEDs with High Speed, Enhanced Gap Tolerance, and High Precision
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Micro light-emitting diodes (micro-LEDs) offer superior performance for next-generation displays, yet their scalable manufacturing is severely bottlenecked by the mass transfer process from donor to receiver substrates. The existing laser-induced forward transfer (LIFT) methods are restricted by low throughput, limited selectivity, and long reaction times. In this study, we introduce a novel defocused direct laser ablation transfer (D-DLAT) method utilizing polyimide as a dynamic release layer. Whereas most indirect laser transfer methods trigger chip release followed by passive descent toward the receiver, D-DLAT directly ablates the release layer to actively propel the small-sized chips towards the receiver via ablation shock. By optimizing the ablation profiles and scanning paths, this method achieves high-speed transfer with significantly enhanced precision and robustness. We demonstrate the successful transfer of micro-LEDs ranging from 600 $\unicode{x03BC}$m down to 35 $\unicode{x03BC}$m in size, with a minimum reported placement error of less than 1 $\unicode{x03BC}$m, and a critical transfer gap of up to 50 $\unicode{x03BC}$m. Furthermore, the D-DLAT approach enables full selectivity, facilitating complex patterned transfers and array repitching operations that are essential for full-color display integration. Our findings indicate that D-DLAT effectively overcomes the fundamental limitations of current transfer technologies, demonstrating substantial potential for the scalable and high-yield manufacturing of advanced micro-LED displays. Ultimately, D-DLAT establishes a robust paradigm for the high-speed manipulation and heterogeneous integration of micro-optoelectronic devices, extending its profound implications beyond displays to the broader landscape of advanced micro-assembly and flexible electronics.

items.title: Optical Coherent Combining in Multi-Aperture Free-Space Receivers through Atmospheric Turbulence via Optically Computed Alignment Gradients
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-aperture reception converts spatial diversity into a coherent-combining gain, but only if the relative phase and polarization of the collected field replicas are aligned before they are summed. In a satellite-to-ground downlink the atmosphere perturbs amplitude, phase and polarization, so the alignment must track a fluctuating channel rather than a fixed offset. This paper proposes a new optical-domain combining scheme in which the alignment information is computed by light itself: the ascent directions that maximize the combined output power are formed by optical interference and read out directly as differential photocurrents of balanced detection, so no estimate of the channel, no deliberate perturbation, and no per-branch digital processing is needed to obtain them. Every branch is aligned against one shared reference - a passive tap of the combined field itself - so no independent laser or optical frequency lock is required, and the update directions of all branches are available simultaneously in a single averaging window without frequency, code, or time multiplexing. The data path needs a single dual-polarization coherent receiver regardless of the aperture count, and the readout is built from elementary parts only - a 3 dB directional coupler, static phase shifters, a Faraday rotator, and balanced photodiodes - so no 90-degree optical hybrid, mixer, or polarization-diverse hybrid is required. The phase and polarization loops are fixed-gain and division-free, and each branch carries one phase modulator and one polarization controller with no amplitude actuator. A closed-form combining-gain and loss budget is derived, the assumptions and limitations of the scheme are stated explicitly, and experimental validation remains open.

items.title: Displacement-noise-free gravitational-wave detector using quantum tomography of photon orbital angular momentum states
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21112v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) induce quantum transitions between photon orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) states with amplitudes $\alpha_{\pm}$. Exploiting this effect, we present a displacement-noise-free detection framework that extracts GW information from the OAM Hilbert space. Parametrized quantum state tomography of the GW-induced OAM sidebands enables a single V-shaped detector to resolve all seven wave parameters: the frequency, propagation direction, two polarization amplitudes, and initial phase of each polarization. Direct detection of the sidebands yields a weak signal of approximately $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{W}$. We therefore introduce a stronger reference state $r |0>_{\mathrm{P}}$, with $r=0.01$, to enhance the detected signal. For an arm length of $L=4\,\mathrm{m}$, $N=160$ round trips, a paraxial parameter of $\gamma=0.1$, an incident light power of $P_{\mathrm{BS}}=10\,\mathrm{kW}$, a wavelength of $\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=1064\,\mathrm{nm}$, and GW amplitudes of $A=10^{-18}$, we estimate sideband transition amplitudes of $|\alpha_{\pm}|\sim10^{-10}$ and signal powers of order $1\,\mathrm{nW}$, scaling as $P_{\mathrm{BS}}\alpha_{\pm}\propto P_{\mathrm{BS}}ANL\gamma/\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}$. The shot-noise-limited sensitivity floor is $S^{1/2}_n=1.6\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{Hz}^{-1/2}$. Because the scheme measures OAM transition amplitudes rather than differential arm lengths, it is intrinsically free from displacement noise and provides a broadband probe of GWs, specifically bridging the $0.1$--$10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ mid-frequency gap.

items.title: Bayesian Joint Reconstruction and Uncertainty Quantification for Limited-Data Multi-Contrast X-Ray CT
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21406v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-contrast X-ray computed tomography (CT) combines attenuation contrast with phase and dark-field contrast, which are sensitive to refraction and ultra-small-angle scattering, respectively. Common implementations record several intensity measurements per projection angle by phase or mask stepping, which lengthens acquisition and, at a fixed exposure per measurement, raises the dose. Limited-data acquisition via sparse angular sampling or reduced stepping lowers these costs but makes the data less informative, calling for prior information and uncertainty quantification. We study joint Bayesian reconstruction of attenuation, phase, and dark-field images from separately retrieved sinograms. A joint total variation term in the prior couples edge locations across the images but not their values. Posterior sampling with the No-U-Turn Sampler complements maximum a posteriori estimates with pixel-wise uncertainty. We compare this joint prior with channel-wise total variation alone on synthetic and experimental Talbot-Lau interferometry data under full, sparse-angle, sparse-step, and combined acquisition (up to 24 times fewer exposures). Both maximum a posteriori reconstructions suppressed undersampling artifacts, with synthetic relative errors 1.6-11 times lower than those of filtered backprojection. The joint prior gave modest synthetic accuracy gains, a cleaner experimental dark-field background, 23-30 % lower mean dark-field posterior standard deviation, and 4-38% higher median effective sample size in experimental limited-data runs. In the synthetic study, posterior standard deviations matched or exceeded the errors in flat regions but underestimated them at boundaries, especially in phase. Experimental phase chains mixed slowly under angular undersampling. The formulation also applies to edge illumination with adapted forward and noise models.

items.title: Imaging defects in two-dimensional crystals by convergent beam electron diffraction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21542v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED), recently demonstrated on two-dimensional (2D) materials, offers a number of interesting applications such as imaging atomic in- and out-of plane shifts, interlayer distances, and individual adsorbates. In this study, we show how CBED allows for atomic-precision imaging of individual defects in 2D materials using one single-shot intensity measurement. In combination with structural calculations using density functional theory, we present simulated CBED patterns for various defects in graphene, each of which exhibits a unique fingerprint distribution. We also show how atomic positions, including the individual atomic defects in graphene, can be reconstructed by iterative phase retrieval from a single CBED pattern.

items.title: Quantum analysis of a multi-frequency laser with a photonic time crystal
items.summary: arXiv:2605.20042v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The present study considers the operation of a laser that incorporates a photonic time crystal (PTC), the purpose of which is to generate a field characterised by multiple widely separated optical frequencies. This laser is the subject of both a proposal and theoretical investigation. The laser comprises an active medium and a PTC within a small cavity constructed from two photonic crystals that are positioned in an overlapping configuration. PTC is modulated by an external field. The spikes in the laser field spectrum are separated by the PTC modulation frequency. The development of a quantum model of the laser with PTC has been achieved, and the analysis of a lasing mode with multi-frequency spikes has been made. The investigation focused on the study of lasing conditions, output power, and the lasing field spectra. The experimental realization of the multi-frequency laser with PTC under realistic conditions is discussed.

items.title: Optical chirality of membrane metasurfaces with broken in-plane symmetry
items.summary: arXiv:2606.05775v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study chiroptical properties of single-layer dielectric membrane metasurfaces with broken in-plane symmetry. Although chiral optics was long tied to structures lacking any mirror symmetry, planar (2D) chiral structures that retain a horizontal mirror plane now attract growing attention for their strong chiral optical effects. We explicitly show and explain how single-layer metasurfaces can achieve strong resonant chiral response. Although the single-layer geometry forbids conventional co-polarized circular dichroism, strong resonant conversion circular dichroism appears to be possible in particular wavelength ranges determined by the spectra of photonic eigenmodes. We explore its origin starting with a $C_4$ rotation-symmetric and in-plane mirror-symmetric membrane metasurface and applying to it various in-plane perturbations. Simultaneous breaking of the in-plane mirror symmetry and lifting the rotation symmetry unlocks resonantly enhanced circular conversion dichroism. We derive selection rules for this effect and trace its origin to eigenmode interference and intercoupling using chiral coupled-mode theory. Material absorption weakens the conversion dichroism produced by modes of opposite up-down parity, but it is essential for that produced by modes of the same parity.

items.title: Beam shifts and eigenpolarisations for the reflection of vortex beams from homogeneous magnetic surfaces
items.summary: arXiv:2606.14100v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Probing surfaces with optical beams is a powerful technique utilised for material characterisation, and more recently, measuring surface magnetisation with vortex beams has opened new avenues by utilising OAM beams for metrology. In this paper, we focus on extending the theoretical framework of unit order vortex beam reflection to spatially homogeneous magnetic surfaces, and derive expressions for the Goos-H\"anchen (GH) and Imbert-Federov (IF) shifts. We calculate closed form expressions for the plane wave eigenpolarisations, polarisations which remain in the same vectorial direction after reflection, for both dielectric and homogeneous magnetic surfaces. These are found by extending the singularimetry formalism for dielectric surfaces, where the position of the phase vortex can be analytically approximated by taking into account the finite beam width, to homogeneous magnetic surfaces. From this we find the eigenpolarisations of the unit order vortex beam for reflection from both dielectric and homogeneous magnetic surfaces. We discuss with relation to the analytical forms of the Jones matrices for GH and IF shifts the additional reflection behaviour observed for homogeneous magnetic surfaces.

items.title: Divergence of Light Wave Amplitudes in an Interface Layer at Critical Conditions
items.summary: arXiv:2606.16841v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The amplitudes of light modes in a homogeneous interface layer are investigated around the critical conditions (CC) in a total reflection geometry. CC occur when the normal wave vector vanishes; the resulting divergence upon variation of the angle of incidence is characterized by a critical exponent -0.5. Absorption replaces the divergence with a finite peak whose width and height are derived analytically. The high relevance of the amplification for Evanescent Wave Dynamic Light Scattering (EWDLS) is demonstrated using published experimental data. The relation to surface plasmon resonance (SPR) is briefly discussed. An outlook connects the amplitude divergence to a critical analysis of the Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA) presented in a companion paper.

items.title: Photon-conserving Raman soliton attractors in focusing and defocusing Kerr media
items.summary: arXiv:2607.05244v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The sign of the Kerr nonlinear coefficient has long been regarded as irrelevant to the direction of the Raman-induced soliton self-frequency shift. Yet the standard generalized nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation (GNLSE) predicts a frequency shift that depends on the sign of the nonlinearity, which leads to an unphysical blue shift in the defocusing case. We resolve this inconsistency by deriving the time-domain form of the photon-conserving GNLSE (pcGNLSE) from its established frequency-domain counterpart. The derivation reveals that photon-number conservation imposes two sign modifications relative to the standard GNLSE: the Raman-shift coefficient acquires the absolute value of the Kerr nonlinear coefficient in place of its signed counterpart, and the self-steepening-Raman dissipation term likewise carries an absolute-value prefactor rather than a signed one. These two modifications jointly guarantee a universal spectral redshift and monotonically decreasing pulse energy during propagation, irrespective of the signs of the Kerr nonlinear coefficient and its frequency derivative. Applying the method of moments to the time-domain pcGNLSE with appropriate chirped ans\"atze, we derive closed-form evolution equations for five pulse parameters and establish explicit attractor conditions under which bright or dark Raman solitons propagate with constant peak power. Direct numerical integration of the pcGNLSE confirms all analytical predictions and demonstrates that the standard GNLSE fails qualitatively, predicting unphysical energy growth and spectral blueshift in the negative-nonlinearity regime. The results provide a rigorous analytical framework for Raman soliton dynamics in materials with negative third-order susceptibility, with direct implications for soliton-based devices in emerging semiconductor waveguide and microresonator platforms.

items.title: f-2f self-referencing for silicon nitride photonics via a heterogeneously integrated lithium niobate layer
items.summary: arXiv:2609.23328v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Heterogeneous integration combines complementary material properties in a single photonic platform. Here, we demonstrate on-chip $f$-2$f$ self-referencing in a heterogeneously integrated Si$_3$N$_4$/LiNbO$_3$ platform, in which supercontinuum generation in a Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguide and second-harmonic generation in a LiNbO$_3$ layer are spatially separated and linked by adiabatic escalator couplers. Pumped by a 1560 nm mode-locked laser with 75 pJ on-chip pulse energy, we detect the carrier-envelope offset frequency with 30 dB signal-to-noise ratio in 300 kHz resolution bandwidth. A comparative measurement confirms that the second harmonic originates in the LiNbO$_3$ layer and indicates opportunity for further improvements through periodic poling. These results establish heterogeneous Si$_3$N$_4$/LiNbO$_3$ integration as a viable building block for self-referenced ultrafast pulse sources in low-loss Si$_3$N$_4$ photonics.

items.title: Time-Rescaled STIRAP Enables Compact Cascaded Frequency Conversion
items.summary: arXiv:2602.18930v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this letter we explore how full frequency conversion can be performed in shorter optical devices by using a STIRAP-like protocol modified by the time rescaling shortcut to adiabaticity. We first show a detailed, step-by-step process of how the coupled equations for two simultaneous three-wave mixing processes can be written in terms of a STIRAP-like system. From the properties of the STIRAP protocol, we know that the ensuing process will result in robust conversion, but require long propagation distances inside the bulk crystal or waveguide. We then apply the time rescaling shortcut to adiabaticty in the conversion process to create a TR-STIRAP protocol, showing that full and robust conversion is also obtained, but at a fraction of the propagation distance. We also show how the original shaping of the coupling coefficients required by the TR-STIRAP can be approximated by Gaussian functions with high conversion fidelity, thus simplifying the experimental implementation. Finally, a possible application of the new protocol is discussed in the context of single-photon detection in the MIR.

items.title: Domain of Applicability of the Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA): A Critical Analysis for X-ray and Visible-Light Interface Scattering
items.summary: arXiv:2610.14054v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Distorted Wave Born Approximation (DWBA) is established for X-ray interface scattering, yet its domain of applicability has never been stated explicitly. The DWBA implicitly rests on the small refractive index deviation (SRID) condition - satisfied by X-rays ($|n-1| \sim 10^{-6}$) but violated by visible light ($|n-1| \sim 0.5$). The DWBA mixes microscopic and macroscopic Maxwell equations, whereas a rigorous optical theory must be built on the macroscopic Maxwell equations and constitutive relations. Rigorous alternatives for two specific inconsistencies in the standard DWBA are discussed. The Extended Transfer Matrix Approach (ETMA) for visible-light interface scattering is outlined.

items.title: Thermal Confinement in Plasmonic Nanoparticles under Generalised Pulsed Illumination
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermal confinement is a key parameter in photothermal applications, as it determines the spatial extent of the region affected by the generated heat. In this work, we develop a numerical treatment to quantify thermal confinement in spherical plasmonic nanoparticles under excitation conditions ranging from ultrashort pulses to the continuous-wave regime. The model combines generalized optical heating with a finite-difference solution of the transient heat equation and explicitly accounts for finite interfacial thermal conductance. To characterize the spatial distribution of heat, we introduce a thermal confinement radius defined from the temporal temperature envelope in the surrounding medium. We demonstrate that pulse duration acts as a highly effective, tuneable parameter to govern thermal confinement. Notably, we quantitatively show that finite interfacial thermal conductance can induce deviations of up to 20% in the spatial confinement radius and over 60% in the transient thermal construct under ultrashort excitation. By comparing the characteristic dimensions of representative targeting ligands with the resulting thermal-confinement length scales, we show how pulse duration can be precisely tailored to control target heating. These results provide a unified framework for predicting nanoscale heat localization paving the way for the rational design of high precision thermoplasmonic applications.

items.title: Molecule-by-molecule nanoresolved picosecond Purcell-enhanced emission at room-temperature in hollow plasmonic nanocone metamaterials
items.summary: arXiv:2506.15095v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nanoscale variations in the electromagnetic environment strongly influence quantum emission processes, yet direct quantitative visualization of these effects at the single-emitter level remains challenging. By combining single-molecule super-resolution microscopy with time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC), we read the local electromagnetic environment of each molecule from its position and its excited-state lifetime. Using wafer-scale arrays of hollow plasmonic nanocones, we map position-dependent variations in the local density of optical states (LDOS) along the nanocone axis. We observe pronounced LDOS gradients that evidence a shortening of the fluorescence lifetime from nanoseconds to few picoseconds. The measured decay rates along the nanocone axis with maximum value at the top ring, yielding a total spontaneous-emission rate enhancement of more than two orders of magnitude at the single-molecule level, reaching an enhancement of the total spontaneous-emission rate of up to two orders of magnitude at the single-molecule level, in agreement with numerical simulations. These results provide direct experimental access to three-dimensional electromagnetic landscapes and establish a non-perturbative platform for quantitative molecular nanosensing in complex photonic architectures. The approach opens new opportunities for engineered room-temperature photon sources, vectorial field sensing, and scalable integrated nanophotonic technologies.

items.summary: When light hits a tiny defect embedded in a solid material like diamond or silicon carbide, it can kick the defect's electrons into an excited state. These spin defects have the potential to be used as stable, readable qubits for quantum technologies, for example, quantum sensing. But modeling the full physics of their energetics over time—a key step in developing spin defects into new technologies—is a challenging task.

items.summary: Nature Photonics, Published online: 13 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02025-8 The nonlinear high harmonic circular dichroism for crystals with broken time-reversal symmetry is found to be directly proportional to the local Berry curvature, and it can be directly probed via ultrafast all-optical measurements.

items.title: Quantum sensor could measure how Earth drags spacetime
items.summary: Einstein's theory of general relativity describes gravity as the bending of spacetime, a mathematical model that combines three-dimensional space and time into a single, four-dimensional continuum. The theory also predicts that a rotating object, such as Earth, slightly drags the surrounding spacetime as it rotates, a phenomenon known as frame-dragging.

items.title: Megabar Shocks on a Benchtop
items.summary: arXiv:2610.20749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Techniques to generate megabar (100 GPa) pressure are critical for the study of materials under extreme conditions. However, kJ-class lasers are typically needed to generate such extreme pressures. Here, we present a method to reach megabar pressure on a benchtop using only tens of mJ a few millijoules of laser pulse energy. The core of our method is the utilization of multiple laser rings of different diameters and time delays to additively excite a focusing shock wave. Using high-speed imaging and a streak camera, we measured the shock trajectory and inferred pressure, temperature and density using hydrocode simulation. Our shock compression efficiency, informed by hydrocode, has achieved 23 GPa/mJ. If scaled up, our method may enable high-energy-density experiments on a benchtop.

items.title: Nonreciprocal Control of Spatiotemporal Floquet Dynamics in Levitated Optomechanical Arrays
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodically driven photonic and optomechanical systems provide a versatile setting for realizing collective Floquet dynamics, yet the relation between temporal locking and continuous rotation of the finite-$q$ pattern remains poorly understood. We show that a nonreciprocal ring of parametrically driven optically levitated particles allows the spatial phase to be controlled while collective temporal locking is preserved. Nonreciprocity polarizes the counterpropagating finite-wave-vector modes and drives a transition from the pinned state to persistent directional spatial-phase drift. The normalized spatial-phase drift velocity is independently encoded in the splitting of the two dominant spectral branches, and its direction reverses with the coupling asymmetry. The pinned regime exhibits a laboratory frame period-two time-crystalline response, whereas the rotating regime forms a distinct temporally locked spatiotemporally ordered state. The same correspondence between spatial-phase drift and spectral splitting persists down to few-particle rings, indicating that the effect does not require a large array. These results establish nonreciprocity as a route to independently control spatial-phase drift and temporal synchronization in driven levitated optomechanical systems.

items.title: Watt-level single-cavity dual-comb laser at 2.1 mum wavelength
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compact ultrafast laser combs around the 2 $\mu$m atmospheric transmission window are of growing interest for direct spectroscopy and as drivers for nonlinear conversion to otherwise hard-to-reach spectral regions. Dual-comb systems in this region remain very scarce: existing implementations rely mostly on nonlinear conversion, resulting in complex systems with poor conversion efficiency and overall low average and peak power. In this paper, we report on a watt-level dual-comb laser directly emitting at 2.1 $\mu$m. The system is based on a single-cavity, soft-aperture Kerr-lens mode-locked (KLM) laser using a broadband holmium (Ho)-doped CaAlGdO$_4$ (CALGO) gain crystal. The laser delivers a total output power exceeding 2 W (1 W per comb) with a sub-100-fs pulse duration (50 nm bandwidth) at a repetition rate of 96.5 MHz, corresponding to a pulse energy of 10 nJ and a peak power of 100 kW per comb. To assess the source's potential for future spectroscopic applications, we characterize the free-running dual comb in detail for frequency stability, phase noise, and relative intensity noise (RIN), and benchmark the achievable spectral resolution by measuring spectral modulations imposed by Fabry-P\'erot etalons. Our system combines the compactness, high efficiency, and passive mutual coherence of a single-cavity oscillator with watt-level average power at 2.1 $\mu$m, making it a promising source for environmental sensing in the atmospheric transmission window, or as a driver for nonlinear frequency conversion, for example, to the MIR and THz regions.

items.title: Frequency comb stability, bistability, and self-starting in normal dispersion microresonators
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that it is possible to generate frequency combs in normal dispersion microresonators by taking advantage of fabricated mode coupling that induces a mode split. In particular, photonic crystal resonators periodically modulate the microresonator's width, which geometrically creates mode coupling. In contrast to frequency combs generated by microresonators in the anomalous dispersion regime, which are typically generated using bright solitons, the frequency combs generated by normal dispersion regime microresonators are dark pulses that are commonly referred to as dark solitons or platicons. In this work, we examine the linear stability of platicons in the pump-detuning and pump-power parameter space as the mode split strength and cavity dispersion is varied. Our work reveals a broad region of stability for platicons. Our work also reveals the existence of fingers at high power at whose boundaries a sharp transition occurs and inside of which platicon solutions are bistable. Finally, we investigate the overlap of the region where platicons are stable with the region where continuous waves are modulationally unstable, and it is possible for a platicon to self-start. Simulations show that platicons consistently self-start inside this region.

items.title: Casimir forces on suspended thin dielectric membranes covered with graphene
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21437v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the Casimir force on thin suspended dielectric layers covered with graphene, both theoretically and experimentally. Thermal effects of the Casimir force on graphene occur at separations significantly smaller compared to ordinary metals and dielectrics. At such small separations, the Casimir force is sufficiently strong to be measured experimentally. However, the presence of substrates to support the graphene significantly reduces the enhancement. We show theoretically that replacing the solid substrate beneath graphene with a thin dielectric membrane partially restores this strong thermal dependence. One of the interacting objects is a solid gold plate. The other object is a suspended dielectric membrane made of either 15 nm of silicon oxide or 13 nm silicon nitride, covered with graphene. At a separation of $\sim$500 nm, theoretical predictions yield changes in the Casimir pressure of up to 54 % and 40 % for silicon oxide and silicon nitride, respectively, when the temperature is increased from 10 K to 294 K. Measurements were performed for graphene on a suspended silicon nitride membrane at room temperature, using a gold-coated sphere attached to a cantilever as the force sensor. The measured force gradient is consistent with the theoretical prediction, although the thermal dependence could not be resolved, in part because of uncertainties in the optical properties of silicon nitride. Replacing a bulk substrate with a thin dielectric membrane covered with graphene provides a substantial reduction of the Casimir force, which may facilitate the stable operation of neutral nanomechanical elements at small separations.

items.title: Chiroptical Nonlinearity Found in Covalent Organic Frameworks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.13728v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chiroptical nonlinearity is vital for modern optics and photonics. However, it remains a central challenge to obtain a material simultaneously with large second-order nonlinearity and strong nonlinear optical chirality. Here we uncover the strong chiroptical nonlinearity in COF-330-a, owing to the formation of unique chiral, polar structure with large p-electron conjugation via structural transformation. A large effective second-order nonlinear susceptibility of ~ 101 pm/V and a strong nonlinear chiroptical response (SHG-CD: -1.60 to +1.66) have been demonstrated in individual COF-330-a microcrystals, transcending the performance trade-off limitation in conventional chiroptical materials. These findings open a new avenue for designing nonlinear chiroptical materials which harness the duality of polarity and chirality and chemical versatility of COFs.

items.title: When is vaccine prioritization worth optimizing?
items.summary: arXiv:2607.00484v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optimizing vaccine prioritization is often treated as the default policy response when vaccine supply is limited. Yet optimized prioritization carries administrative, ethical and communication costs, motivating an upstream question: whether differences among vaccine allocations can alter epidemic outcomes enough to make optimization epidemiologically necessary. We show that optimization is not always worth pursuing: in some regimes, vaccination markedly reduces epidemic burden, but many feasible allocation rules perform almost equally well, making the necessity of optimization low. We quantify this necessity as the range of epidemic outcomes generated by different allocations under fixed supply and show that it is governed by competition between vaccinating high-contact groups to slow transmission and vaccinating groups that benefit most directly: necessity is low when these protection routes are balanced and high when one dominates. Increasing transmission intensity changes this balance and drives a transition in the optimal allocation from transmission-focused prioritization toward direct protection. Different prevention objectives exhibit distinct transition thresholds, creating regimes in which optimizing one objective substantially compromises another, thereby revealing when the choice of prevention target matters most. This framework reframes vaccine prioritization as a prior decision problem, identifying when optimization is warranted, when simpler rules suffice, and when prevention goals conflict.

items.title: Ultrashort laser pulses offer a new way to probe electrons' quantum geometry
items.summary: Researchers at Friedrich Schiller University Jena and the University of Regensburg have developed a method for determining, using light, a quantum property of electrons that has hitherto been difficult to access. The focus is on what is known as Berry curvature—a quantity that describes certain geometric properties of the quantum mechanical states of electrons. The researchers measured it in a layer of the semiconductor tungsten diselenide, just one atomic layer thick, using ultrashort laser pulses. items.title: Engineering Multipole Resonances in Dielectric Metasurfaces for Transmission, Reflection, and Absorption Control
items.summary: Dielectric metasurfaces have moved to the forefront of nanophotonics, offering flat, low-loss alternatives to conventional bulk optical elements for controlling the amplitude, phase, and polarization of light. These structures are of growing interest to researchers and engineers working on sensing, energy harvesting, and flat optics, as their performance hinges on precisely engineered optical resonances. Full-wave finite element simulation, combined with semianalytical multipole decomposition in the COMSOL Multiphysics® software, gives us a way to not only predict these resonances but also uncover their underlying physical origins. In this webinar, Dr. Pavel Terekhov, postdoctoral researcher at National Institute of Standards and Technology, will trace how a single quadrumer meta-atom, originally studied for its magnetic octupole response, evolves into two distinct light manipulation regimes. He will first revisit the foundational single-particle results that motivated this work, then show how arranging quadrumers into a periodic crystalline silicon metasurface produces anomalous absorption enhancement, governed by two independent multipole mechanisms coexisting in the same structure. Building on this, he will then introduce ongoing work on a gallium nitride metasurface, where the complex interplay of four different multipoles is used to sculpt reflection and transmission spectra including the quasi-bound-states-in-the-continuum (q-BIC) manipulation. Attendees will see how COMSOL Multiphysics® and multipole decomposition connect full-wave simulation and analytical insight, turning abstract resonance behavior into physically interpretable design rules. The broader takeaway is that multipole-based simulation is not just a diagnostic tool but a design strategy: It enables the on-demand tailoring of absorption, reflection, and transmission in dielectric metasurfaces, with direct relevance to sensing, energy harvesting, and future optical device applications. items.topic_title: Using quantum entanglement to probe hidden properties of quarks
items.zh_full: 据Physics World报道，两个相距约一米的超导量子比特被驱动进入纠缠态，而这一纠缠并非尽管存在环境噪声，而是由环境噪声促成。文章标题为“Noise that entangles may accelerate the dawn of quantum technologies”，指出噪声在特定条件下可能成为促成量子纠缠的因素，而非单纯的干扰源。该结果的意义在于，如果环境噪声可以被利用来辅助或加速量子纠缠的建立，可能为量子技术的早期发展提供新的思路。报道强调，这一现象发生在两个超导量子比特之间，二者通过约一米的线缆连接。文章认为，这种由噪声促成的纠缠可能有助于推动量子技术走向实用化阶段。
